facts.text: Ignaz Semmelweis was a Hungarian doctor who worked at the Vienna General Hospital in Austria in the 1840s.
The hospital had two maternity wards: one run by male doctors and medical students, the other by female midwives.
Women in the doctors' ward died of childbed fever at more than twice the rate of women in the midwives' ward.
Doctors and students went from autopsies to the maternity ward without washing their hands; the midwives did not do autopsies.
In 1847 Semmelweis made handwashing compulsory for the doctors and students in his ward.
He used a chlorinated lime solution instead of plain soap because it removed the smell of decay from their hands.
After the rule began, deaths in the doctors' ward fell sharply.
His theory was rejected; historians think one reason was that it implied doctors themselves were responsible for patients dying.
The Vienna hospital later dropped the handwashing rule.
Semmelweis died in 1865, before his ideas were accepted.
In 1867, two years after his death, Joseph Lister began promoting the cleaning of hands and surgical tools; surgeons began scrubbing before operations regularly in the 1870s.
The medical university in Budapest was renamed Semmelweis University in his honor.
Global Handwashing Day is held every year on October 15.
Studies show handwashing can prevent about 1 in 3 diarrhea-related illnesses and 1 in 5 respiratory infections such as colds.
